node.label: Allan Greer
node.date_label: “Fur-Trade Labour” 1981 · “A Critique of Pentland” and Peasant, Lord, and Merchant 1985 · Colonial Leviathan (ed. with Radforth) 1992 · The Patriots and the People 1993 · Property and Dispossession 2018 · “Settler Colonialism and Beyond” 2019
node.description: A historian of Lower Canada and colonial North America whose rural social history described a feudal, household-centred habitant society: in 1985 he held that Lower Canadian 'agriculture was organized primarily around the satisfaction of family subsistence needs through family production', with part of the surplus 'diverted to priests and seigneurs through feudal exactions', a view he set against both Ouellet's routine-bound peasant (1981) and the commercial farmer of Paquet and Wallot, while allowing that 'Feudal peasants or market-conscious farmers? No doubt the debates will continue' (1985). The same essay, a critique of Clare Pentland's Labour and Capital in Canada, faulted the staples tradition of Innis and Creighton for confining attention to 'relations of exchange'. With Ian Radforth he edited Colonial Leviathan (1992), on mid-nineteenth-century state formation, which Bryan Palmer found to lack coherence (1993) and which Greer later said 'neglected everything to do with Indigenous peoples and processes of elimination' (2019); his history of the 1837 rebellion (1993) is known here through reviewers, who read it as breaking with Ouellet's manipulated peasantry. His later work on 'property formation' (2018) and his 2019 lecture treat settler colonialism as one mode of colonial invasion among several, 'a dominant force in some periods and regions' that 'fades to insignificance in others', while insisting 'I am not here to trash or dismiss settler-colonial theory'.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Allan Greer (b. 1950); “Fur-Trade Labour and Lower Canadian Agrarian Structures” (1981); “Wage Labour and the Transition to Capitalism: A Critique of Pentland” (Labour/Le Travail, 1985); Peasant, Lord, and Merchant: Rural Society in Three Quebec Parishes, 1740–1840 (1985); ed. with Ian Radforth, Colonial Leviathan: State Formation in Mid-Nineteenth-Century Canada (1992); The Patriots and the People: The Rebellion of 1837 in Rural Lower Canada (1993; French translation Habitants et Patriotes, 1997); “Commons and Enclosure in the Colonization of North America” (2012); Property and Dispossession: Natives, Empires and Land in Early Modern North America (2018); “Settler Colonialism and Beyond” (2019). Further selected bibliography: Mohawk Saint: Catherine Tekakwitha and the Jesuits (2005); The People of New France (1997); Ed., The Jesuit Relations: Natives and Missionaries in Seventeenth-Century North America (2000); “1837–38: Rebellion Reconsidered” (1995); “Colonial Saints: Gender, Race, and Hagiography in New France” (2000).
node.scope_note: This entry presents Greer's account of rural Lower Canada and the transition to capitalism (1981–85), the state-formation collection (1992) and his later historicising of settler colonialism (2018–19). Read on 2026-10-14: 'Wage Labour and the Transition to Capitalism' (1985, pp. 7–22) and 'Settler Colonialism and Beyond' (2019, pp. 61–86) in full; the introduction to Property and Dispossession (2018, pp. 1–24) on Cambridge Core, which shows no page markers; Palmer's 1993 review of Colonial Leviathan in full. 'Fur-Trade Labour' (1981) was read in full for the Ouellet entry and its critique of Ouellet is carried by edge_989, not repeated here. Peasant, Lord, and Merchant (1985) and The Patriots and the People (1993) are unread (lending-only copies); the 1985 book is known from its publisher's description and the 1993 book from reviews. Ouellet's review essay on the 1993 book (Histoire sociale / Social History, 1995) is unread, so no reply by Ouellet is quoted. His New France and Jesuit work (The People of New France, 1997; Mohawk Saint, 2005) is not covered. Canonical-work review (2026-10-24): added titles and dates are selected bibliography, not a complete career or a new reading of the books. Original works, translations, edited collections and posthumous editions are distinguished; earlier argument and source-reading qualifications remain.

incident_edges.relationship: Rural Lower Canada as a feudal, household-centred peasant society, neither routine-bound nor market-rational, into which wage labour in the fur and timber trades was fitted (1981–85); and the rebellion of 1837 as a rural popular movement (1993, known through reviews)
incident_edges.evidence_note: His own words (Labour/Le Travail 15, 1985, read in full): 'my own view is that agriculture was organized primarily around the satisfaction of family subsistence needs through family production. There were surpluses and a portion of these were sold, but a significant proportion was diverted to priests and seigneurs through feudal exactions' (pp. 18–19); against the commercial reading of Paquet and Wallot, cited in n. 16, 'Feudal peasants or market-conscious farmers? No doubt the debates will continue', while 'none of these social formations were dominated by the capitalist mode of production' (p. 19); 'capitalist enterprise had to adapt itself to the prevailing non-capitalist environment' (p. 20); subdivision of holdings followed 'the introduction of domestic industry or of seasonal waged work in the fur or timber trades' (p. 16). Peasant, Lord, and Merchant (1985) is unread; its publisher describes rural Quebec as 'essentially organized around a feudal society', with 'a pronounced pattern of household self-sufficiency' in three Lower Richelieu parishes (lof_greer_1985). His 1981 Sorel study rejected the 'atavistic mentality' explanation of the rural crisis; that critique of Ouellet is carried by edge_989 and is not repeated here. The Patriots and the People (1993) is unread. Reviewers' words, not his: Dessureault (1998, read for evidence-quebec.md) says it 'brise nettement avec les travaux antérieurs de William H. Parker et de Fernand Ouellet pour qui la paysannerie était essentiellement victime de la crise économique et manipulée par des élites ultranationalistes', finds the struggle fed by 'une forme de républicanisme populaire' (p. 206), places Greer 'dans une perspective marxiste anticolonialiste, héritière de l'œuvre pionnière de Stanley B. Ryerson' (p. 205) and objects that he 'réfute l'existence de clivages socio-économiques à l'intérieur même de la paysannerie' (p. 207); Cardinal (1999) writes that 'à plusieurs reprises, A. Greer s'en prend aux arguments de cet historien' (p. 185). Ouellet's review essay on the book (Histoire sociale / Social History 28, 1995) is unread (browser check), so his reply is not quoted and no fernand_ouellet edge is drawn. Rudin (1995) names Greer among the révisionnistes.

incident_edges.relationship: Colonial Leviathan (1992, edited with Ian Radforth): mid-nineteenth-century state formation in the Canadas, written before the framework was named, and later faulted by Greer himself for neglecting Indigenous peoples (2019)
incident_edges.evidence_note: Colonial Leviathan is unread (lending-only copy; the Érudit, Left History and Histoire sociale reviews returned bot checks). In-period reading: Palmer (Labour/Le Travail 31, 1993, read in full) says the volume and Curtis's book 'are searching for the state in pre-Confederation Canada' (p. 365) and finds that 'the collection lacks coherence', while its 'single most important contribution ... also developed by Curtis, is the notion that the coming of ‘responsible government’ actually entailed the subversion of the reform strategy of the 1830s' (p. 366); he names Greer's chapter on the birth of the police (p. 366). Valverde's 1992 essay cites Fecteau's chapter in the volume (edge_966). Greer's own later judgment (2019, read): 'The time may be right, then, for a renewed history of the Confederation era, one that unites the history of state formation with that of settler colonialism' (p. 73), with n. 41: 'A prime example of this problem would be Colonial Leviathan; devoted to questions of state formation, it neglected everything to do with Indigenous peoples and processes of elimination' (p. 84). Comparison only: the volume predates McKay's prospectus (2000), and no checked text by McKay or his commentators names it; Pâquet (2009) links the framework to studies of state formation in general. The atlas's state_formation_roots strand places it there editorially.

incident_edges.relationship: Settler colonialism historicised as one mode of colonial invasion among several, beside imperial/commercial penetration and extractivism, dominant in some periods and regions of northern North America and not others: a sympathetic critique that keeps Wolfe's 'structure, not an event' (2018–19)
incident_edges.evidence_note: His own words, all after 2000 and dated. 'Settler Colonialism and Beyond' (Journal of the CHA 30, 2019, read in full; a CHA keynote): settler colonial theory 'does indeed have much to offer historians', but over 500 years of invasion 'the settler variety stands out as a dominant force in some periods and regions, but it fades to insignificance in others' (p. 62); 'The late Patrick Wolfe, still the most important theorist of settler colonialism' (p. 62); the danger of 'temporal flattening' 'when settler colonialism is casually invoked in ways that suggest a transhistorical, always-already quality' (p. 63); 'Let me assure you that I am not here to trash or dismiss settler-colonial theory' and, with Wolfe, settler colonialism is 'a structure, not an event'; 'However, that doesn't mean we need to find settler colonialism everywhere and all the time' (p. 63); 'Imperial/Commercial Penetration' and 'Extractivism' are 'coexisting and overlapping versions of colonialism' (p. 64); early settlements 'hardly functioned as instruments of elimination and replacement except in quite limited, localized ways' (p. 64); 'To those who insist that Canada is, was, and always has been a settler-colonial phenomenon, I offer qualified support' (p. 73); 'settlers as such are no longer the main threat, for the invasion has adopted a different guise' (p. 74); and 'Settler colonialism stands out also as a fundamental force behind the creation of a territorial nation-state' (p. 79). Property and Dispossession (2018), introduction read on Cambridge Core (no page markers): 'Some scholars speak of an “eliminationist” logic driving settler colonialism ... toward the utter destruction of natives who stand in its way', but 'such “ethnic cleansing” is not the whole story' (n. 25 cites Wolfe 2006). The target is the field, not patrick_wolfe: Greer accepts Wolfe's structure thesis and objects to how the term is commonly used, citing Woolford and Benvenuto's warning that it risks becoming 'a reductive shorthand' (p. 63). The William and Mary Quarterly essay (2019) is unread beyond its recorded opening.

incident_edges.relationship: In a critique of Pentland's Labour and Capital in Canada, the staples tradition's trade-centred economy faulted for confining attention to relations of exchange and passing over the household subsistence production that, he argued, made up most of early Canada's economy (1985)
incident_edges.evidence_note: His own words (Labour/Le Travail 15, 1985, read in full), in a critique of H. C. Pentland's Labour and Capital in Canada, 1650–1860 (written 1960, published 1981), which is not an atlas entry: Pentland 'follows the lead of his Toronto mentors in conflating the Canadian economy and its overseas trade'; 'While Innis, Creighton, and their contemporary disciples confine their attention to relations of exchange, however, Pentland at least focuses on the ‘social relations of production’', so 'it seems fair to regard him as the labour historian of the staples school' (p. 9). The subsistence producers who were most of the population 'were therefore scarcely of interest to bourgeois theorists from Adam Smith to Harold Innis and Clare Pentland. For these last two, ‘the colonial economy’ meant the meagre flow of commodities' (p. 21). His counter-claim is stated as an untested estimate: 'No one has yet made a serious attempt to measure the value of the colony's annual production of all goods'; 'If they did, I have no doubt that the aggregate agricultural output would embody vastly more labour than all the furs and squared timbers and other ‘staple products’' (p. 20). Qualifications kept: Pentland 'deserves high marks for posing the important questions and for assembling valuable information' (p. 8). The arrow stands for this passage of a review essay aimed chiefly at Pentland; Greer names Innis and Creighton as the staples school but does not review their books. Note 2 (p. 8) also discusses Kealey's and Palmer's use of Pentland; that is not drawn as an edge.

named_group_routes.evidence_note: Weaver relates property rights to the growth of democracy and the market economy; Heaman places "the propertied versus the people" at the centre of Canadian political history; Greer studies property formation. named_group_routes.relationship: Relations and encounter versus a structure of dispossession
named_group_routes.evidence_note: The same archives and subjects (reserves, schools, policy) are read as relations and encounter here and as a continuing settler structure in the Settler colonialism entry. named_group_routes.relationship: Canada as a project of liberal rule: the prospectus of 2000
named_group_routes.evidence_note: In-period evidence (2000). The prospectus abstract (read) proposes mapping 'the Canadian state as a project of liberal rule in northern North America' to get beyond the 'socio-cultural versus national-political impasse'. Its core formulation (pp. 620–21) is checked as quoted by Fecteau (2009): 'Canada-as-project can be analyzed through the study of the implantation and expansion over a heterogeneous terrain of a certain politico-economic logic – to wit liberalism.' The prospectus body is not read here. McKay's spring 2000 Acadiensis essay (pp. 90–91, read) sets out the same programme in his own words: 'a strategy of reconnaissance'; the project 'was the project of liberal order, a coherent attempt to install a liberal public philosophy and practice of "peace, order and good government" in northern North America'; 'Canada was thus a process, not a self-evident thing, and the key to this process was liberalization'. A contribution, not a founding: state-formation studies (Curtis 1988; Greer and Radforth 1992) precede it, and Pâquet (2009) names Gramsci and Fernande Roy (1988) as its sources. In the sampled corpus, 90 of 1,303 strict History doctoral dissertations dated 2009–2026 cite the prospectus. Bibliographies record consultation, not influence. The 2009 reply and the histories of the left (2005, 2008) are later readings, not evidence for this edge.

named_group_routes.relationship: Liberalism read as a system of moral regulation and the liberal state as a constitutor of subjectivities (1991–92), beside the liberal order framework's later history of property, the individual and rule
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Her own in-period statements, before McKay's prospectus (2000). 'Pauperism, Moral Character, and the Liberal State', Labour/Le Travail 30 (1992), pp. 213–222, read in full, endorses Mitchell Dean's argument 'that classical English liberalism was not a negation of state regulation but rather a particular system of economic, social, and moral regulation', so that 'a history of pauperism is also a genealogy of liberalism' (p. 217). She reviews Jean-Marie Fecteau's Un nouvel ordre des choses (1989) as 'a landmark work' whose 'theoretical sophistication' crosses 'the traditional historiographical boundaries separating coercion from benevolence and the state as a whole from charity' (pp. 221–222), but faults its 'moyens de contrôle' as 'a rather functionalist formulation', a 'model of negative class power', and adds that 'These moral codes are not intrinsic to the logic of capital, since capitalism works quite efficiently in different cultural systems' (p. 222). Note 10 (p. 220) cites Fecteau's essay in Greer and Radforth's Colonial Leviathan (1992), and the essay thanks Allan Greer for comments on a draft (p. 222). In the 1991 book (Google Books search-within snippets of the 2008 reissue, 1991 pagination) note 35 (p. 171) cites Bruce Curtis's 'Preconditions of the Canadian State', and she writes that moral regulation 'might be an important social process, which is intertwined with but is not an effect of either the economic or the political' (p. 165) and that 'one has to be sceptical of any claims that envision a clear separation between moral and economic regulation' (p. 166). Reviewers read the book's state argument in the same terms: private philanthropy 'allowed liberal democratic states to adhere to their policy of non-interference in the private sphere' (Loo 1992, p. 278, her paraphrase). Comparison only. The user decided (2026-10-12) that the liberal order framework is 'a different project closer to history of capitalism'; Fecteau and Curtis are shared ground (state formation), not membership. No in-period text by the framework's authors discussing her was read here (McKay's 2000 prospectus is paywalled and unread). edge_848 (liberal_order_framework – moral_regulation) is the field-level comparison. This edge is an editorial comparison of her 1992 argument with the later framework (McKay, 2000); she did not distinguish herself from a framework not yet formulated.

named_group_routes.relationship: The agricultural-crisis thesis and its portrait of a routine-bound peasantry rejected by Paquet and Wallot (1972), criticised from Montreal by Tousignant (1980) and answered by Greer (1981; and in his 1993 book, as characterised by Dessureault, 1998, and Cardinal, 1999)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: This arrow represents Paquet and Wallot's, Tousignant's and Greer's specified interventions in the agricultural-crisis debate (quebec_historiography/agricultural_crisis_debate), not a verdict of the field, which includes Ouellet and his supporters. Paquet and Wallot (RHAF 1972, read in full): of the 1962 article, 'Cet article contient bien plus une intuition qu'une démonstration' (p. 193); Ouellet's postulates include 'le conservatisme invétéré des habitants, nous dirions même leur irrationalité' (p. 195); 'Comme la plupart de ses prédécesseurs, Ouellet peint les habitants comme des paysans essentiellement conservateurs, peu enclins à innover et désespérément embourbés dans des traditions routinières. Il s'agit là, nous semble-t-il, d'une simplification trop fréquente dans l'historiographie et qui appelle des réserves sérieuses' (pp. 201–202); 'Il n'existe pas de rationalité illimitée' (p. 202); 'les habitants ont adopté un régime agraire rationnel' (p. 221); their alternative, the Canadiens as 'd'astucieux politiques' in an 'équilibre conflictuel' with the British party (pp. 235–236), sought 'au-delà d'un économisme grossier' (p. 236); verdict, 'renvoyer comme irrecevable la thèse Ouellet' (p. 237), with the qualification that 'Quant à savoir si le débat est résolu pour autant, nous ne saurions le dire' (p. 237). Pierre Tousignant (RHAF 1980, read in full), on Le Bas-Canada (1976): the 1966 book 'faisait écho aux vieux préjugés de l'historiographie canadienne-anglaise tout imprégnée de l'idéologie de supériorité de la race anglo-saxonne', but the approach 'qui justifiait la notion désormais dépassée du «retard des mentalités» n'apparaît plus au premier plan dans Le Bas-Canada. C'est une notable amélioration' (p. 416); the periodisation of the export series 'n'est évidemment pas innocent' (p. 417); 'Il ne saurait plus être question de porter au seul compte d'une différence de mentalités l'appauvrissement progressif de la majeure partie de la paysannerie' (p. 419); 'Le professeur Ouellet nourrit de telles préventions contre le parti patriote qu'il a développé des réflexes défensifs à l'égard du parti bureaucrate' (p. 430); yet the book gives 'une intelligibilité vivante' to the period (p. 436, after Nicole Gagnon). Allan Greer (CHA Historical Papers 1981, read in full; n. 41 cites Ouellet's Lower Canada, 1980): 'The dominant explanation of Lower Canada's rural crisis emphasizes two factors, one demographic, the other cultural ... the atavistic mentality of the French-Canadian habitants led to their irrational refusal to accept technical improvements' (p. 213); 'The case of Sorel seems to challenge both elements of this interpretation'; 'To echo the commercial bourgeoisie of Lower Canada in blaming the habitants for their own agrarian predicament would be adding ideological insult to economic injury' (p. 214). On the rebellion, Greer's 1993 book is unread; reviewers say (their words): it 'brise nettement avec les travaux antérieurs de William H. Parker et de Fernand Ouellet pour qui la paysannerie était essentiellement victime de la crise économique et manipulée par des élites ultranationalistes' (Dessureault 1998, p. 206); 'à plusieurs reprises, A. Greer s'en prend aux arguments de cet historien, selon lesquels les habitants canadiens-français avaient une mentalité arriérée' (Cardinal 1999, p. 185). Ouellet's reply (1976, read): his critics 'ont réduit notre analyse à un simple rapport entre nationalisme et malaise agricole' and made the debate 'presque stérile' (p. 116); 'Le débat ne mérite plus d'être poursuivi; c'est la recherche qui exige de l'être' (p. 132). Le Goff's review of the controversy (CHR 1974) is unread; Ouellet reports that it concluded for a crisis from the early nineteenth century (1985, p. 25), so Le Goff is not counted among these critics.

named_group_routes.relationship: Palmer questions treating Curtis’s school-inspection study as a representative model of Canadian state formation, while crediting its revision of responsible government.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Fresh primary review, 1993, printed 365–367: Palmer finds the inspection focus too narrow and its model overstated, but acknowledges useful evidence and the responsible-government argument. His separate criticism of Greer and Radforth’s edited collection retains its own subject; the entire joint review is not assigned to Curtis. Curtis’s 1992 book remains unread.
